title: Ladybird's first alpha release
content:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.

This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):

Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude):

Ladybird (72925)  [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926)  [61 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72927)  [29 MB]
    ├── ProcessReaper (72928)  [1 MB]
    ├── Compositor (72930)  [123 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72953)  [36 MB]
    ├── WebContent (72984)  [819 MB]
    ├── MediaServer (73006)  [118 MB]
    ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007)  [20 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73052)  [144 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73057)  [73 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73073)  [166 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73094)  [70 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73112)  [116 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (73113)  [27 MB]
    └── WebContent (73185)  [60 MB]

Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).

I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool. It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.

The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite, which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:

undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')

I filed an issue about this, then found a FIXME annotation in the source code.

The October explosion

The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.

Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months:

That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.

This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark, they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari!

How did they do that? Coding agents:

Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.

I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.

Should you use Ladybird?

Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.

I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

Tags: browsers, open-source, ai, rust, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, andreas-kling, ladybird, coding-agents

The Debt Trap (permalink)

Smoking is very stupid. I was a smoker for 17 years, from ages 13-30. I was very stupid to start smoking. That stupidity only came into sharper focus a few years ago, when I got a cancer diagnosis (don't worry, I am now cancer-free):

https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail

In my defense, I'll point out that I was just a kid when I started, but also, smoking belongs to a class of pernicious problems whose insidiousness is rooted in the distance between their causes and effects:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/

I've often said that if a little tumor had sprouted immediately after I took my first puff, I never would have taken a second one. Now that I've actually had the experience of being told that I have a tumor, I can say definitively that I would not have taken that second puff. An economist would tell you that I was engaged in "hyperbolic discounting": underpricing a future cost and overvaluing a present pleasure:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting

But I don't think that tells the whole story. Sure, I was engaged in hyperbolic discounting, but why was I doing that? What was it about smoking (as opposed to, say, French-kissing light-sockets) that led me to apply a hyperbolic discount to the costs of smoking? I say it was the attenuated relationship between cause and effect. It's not just that we undervalue the price of smoking: it's that we struggle to arrive at a correct price for smoking in the moment, because the intellectual knowledge of cancer statistics is in no way comparable to the visceral experience of a cancer diagnosis. Estimating the "cost" (emotional, physiological, monetary) of a cancer diagnosis is hard, especially if you're young and have had the good fortune of a life untouched by close contact with agonizing illness and death.

The point I'm making is that the discount isn't just hyperbolic, it's hyperbolic because it relies so much upon guesswork, without comparable experiences to anchor your estimate.

What's more, it's this same attenuated causality (in which cause is separated from effect by so much time and space) that allowed the tobacco industry to sow so much profitable doubt about the connection between smoking and cancer. Sure, some of the policymakers who let Big Tobacco off the hook were doubtlessly in their pocket, reliant on campaign contributions or beholden to a party that was in some queasy, cozy relationship with these death merchants. But the reason Big Tobacco was able (is able) to get away with killing us for so many decades is that you don't get a tumor with each puff.

I believe that most of the policymakers who reasoned their way into doubting the connection between smoking and cancer were ensnared by this attenuated causality. They might have had low morals and low intellect, but the factor that made them such easy marks for Big Tobacco's death-hustlers was this wide, long gap between cause and effect.

This cuts both ways: if you're a policymaker of low intellect and morals, you can rig your policies to put their consequences a long way off in the future, which might give you time to escape to a lucrative private-sector career with the industrial interests who benefited from your chicanery. Or (if you're a Mitch McConnell-adjacent flesh-eating ghoul who plans to die only after centuries in office, chin red and slick with the heartblood of the innocent), you can put so much time and space between your fuckery and the ruin it brings that the voting public fails to connect your actions with the consequences. After all, no one ever lost money betting against the American public's object permanence.

For example, Trump's Big Bill was designed to make its deepest cuts – to Medicaid, rural hospitals, the increased tax-load on workers to advantage their bosses – after the midterm elections. The cynical reasoning isn't hard to follow: We'll just tell voters that all the bad things they've been told about the coming cuts are Fake News, and then, after the cuts arrive, blame their post-midterm misery on Biden, communists, trans people, immigrants, and the phases of the moon.

This cheap trick may be deplorable, but you should also save some anger for politicians who enact good policies but refuse to take account of this principle. Take Biden's 2021 plan to lower prescription drug prices. This started off as a rule that would end the longstanding, outrageous policy that bans Medicare/Medicaid from negotiating with pharma companies. Yes, you read that right: when Uncle Sucker buys drugs from Big Pharma, the government just asks the pharma companies how much public money they'd like, and then the USA writes the companies a check for whatever sum they name, no questions asked. That's why the US pays 300% more than any other advanced nation for its drugs.

Thus Biden's initial proposal: let Medicare/Medicaid negotiate drug prices the same way every private insurer and every public health system does. But then, Biden's team allowed that policy to be diluted so that it would only apply to ten drugs, and only if those drugs had been on the market for at least 13 years. Finally, the piece de resistance: the plan wasn't design to kick in until 2025, after the 2024 election, which turned out to be a referendum on the cost of living (including drug prices) that saw the Dems getting their asses kicked by the stupidest, most obviously corrupt fascists in American electoral history:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/11/18/bipartisan-consensus/#corruption

Whether you're ignoring attenuated causality or weaponizing it, it's critical to any analysis of how we get into as much trouble as we do. It is the ruin of individuals and firms, and of political and economic systems.

Take vaccinations: herd immunity requires a lot of compliance: nearly all of us have to get vaccinated before the real benefits kick in. Securing this compliance takes a lot of effort, because the system has to get people to invest their faith in the prospect that eventually we'll get to herd immunity and an end to infection.

But once herd immunity is in place, noncompliance is a much smaller deal. The very fact of herd immunity means that people can opt out here or there without getting sick (because we're all up-to-date on our vaccinations). Worse, the very fact of herd immunity means that after a while, no one can really remember what the sickness was like: we think of measles as something the Little Rascals pretended to have so they could play hooky, not as a terrifyingly infectious disease that can leave you blind or brain damaged. Asking someone who's never lived through a measles epidemic to estimate the cost of measles is like asking a 13 year old to estimate what a cancer diagnosis will feel like.

The same applies to antitrust enforcement. An economy of small and medium sized firms who compete with one another is an economy where workers have more bargaining leverage and regulators don't have to worry about being outspent and outlasted with decade-plus appeals when they crack down on corrupt businesses:

https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/15/business/us-vsibm.html

It's also an economy where companies must compete rather than collude. Look at what happened to the ad-tech industry, which is dominated by a duopoly that controls 80% of display advertising, and that duopoly has an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the market to pay publishers less and charge advertisers more:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue

In the post-war era, antitrust enforcers did their jobs: they blocked mergers, punished predatory pricing, and aggressively investigated sweetheart deals between retail incumbents and their suppliers that were designed to freeze out new businesses:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities

This produced an economy where companies had lower profits, because workers and consumers could force them to disgorge more of their surpluses, and because they had to invest more in improving their offerings to keep up with competitors. It was an economy where prosperity was more broadly shared and where it was easier to impose democratic accountability on the private sector.

Then, starting with Jimmy Carter, America turned its back on antitrust. Year after year, presidency after presidency, enforcers waved through larger and more anticompetitive mergers and ignored more egregious predatory practices. For 50 years, the neoclassical economists who promoted this laissez-faire doctrine have smugly pointed out that even though the economy grew more consolidated thanks to their policy, we still had an economy, one that was often booming, where politicians could (sometimes) be seen to be intervening to address corporate cheating.

The public, meanwhile, has historically struggled to connect the problems of oligarchy with these pro-oligarch policies. They can feel the regulatory capture, they know that labor grows weaker every year, they are furious at their sellout politicians and the system's naked corruption. But because the policy is separated from its outcomes by so much time and space, there's lots of room for the policy's architects and beneficiaries to do the economic version of denying the link between smoking and cancer; that is, denying the link between pro-monopoly policies and monopolies.

Attenuated causality lets bad-faith actors sell us anti-vax, pro-monopoly, cancer denial…and, of course, climate denial. NASA's James Hansen warned Congress about climate change in 1988. It's not like the oil companies didn't know about this. As far back as the 1970s, Exxon's own scientists had warned the company about global warming, and the company took actions based on those warnings:

https://insideclimatenews.org/project/exxon-the-road-not-taken/

Mobil, meanwhile, started secretly raising its drilling platforms to account for rising seas, even as it was taking out full-page ads in national daily newspapers that stated that "The science of climate change is too uncertain to mandate a plan of action":

https://web.archive.org/web/20160101024248/http://graphics.latimes.com/oil-operations/

Attenuated causality was and is at the core of climate denial. If every climate-shredding gas turbine that the self-described environmental hero Elon Musk fired up at one of his AI data-centers immediately caused a flood or a wildfire or a heat-wave, we'd scrape all those data-centers down to their foundation slabs and then we'd display Musk in stocks and pelt him with rotten fruit.

Musk really knows how to turn attenuated causality to his advantage. Remember when he performatively borrowed a security guard's pocket knife and started slicing through the Ethernet cables connecting Twitter's servers?

https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2023-09-14/when-elon-musk-unplugged-the-twitter-servers-with-a-pocket-knife-theres-still-shit-thats-broken-because-of-it.html

Or when he started shutting down whole data-centers and mass-firing Twitter's technical staff?

https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/29/technology/twitter-elon-musk.html

The point of this performance was to let Musk claim that Twitter's management had let itself be gulled by featherbedding engineers who grossly overbuilt Twitter's infrastructure in order to guarantee themselves perpetual employment at the expense of Twitter's shareholders. But all that spare server capacity wasn't excess: it was the cushion, the headroom, the insurance policy. Those were the servers that would pick up the slack when another server lost its power-supply or caught a bad stick of RAM. They were the servers that could shoulder the load during the next 9/11 or Arab Spring. They were the engineering staff that could execute new projects or perform emergency maintenance – and the engineering staff that could plan the next build-out in advance so that future growth wouldn't stall out when Twitter ran out of hardware.

Musk's actions didn't occur in a vacuum. During the decades in which attenuated causality set the scene for an endless, incestuous orgy of mergers and acquisitions, it became normal for business leaders to hack away at their own firms' resiliency. University administrators fired tenured professors and replaced them with casualized, proletarianized adjuncts.

The pedagogy – and the universities' reputations – persisted after the cuts, ebbing away slowly as the institutional memory and standards eroded bit by bit. But eventually, the universities found themselves in crisis. Campuses erupted in student revolt and spectacular scenes of violent repression:

https://jayrosen.tumblr.com/post/13174138991/excerpt-from-uc-davis-2010-2012-general-catalog

Universities' reputations cratered and they found themselves easy pickings for demagogues who awarded themselves a veto over faculty, curriculum and admissions:

https://www.chronicle.com/article/columbia-capitulated-but-so-did-the-rest-of-higher-ed

That's the thing about attenuated causality: it lets people and institutions and systems play a high-stakes game of Jenga in which every non-load-bearing block is removed and added to the top of the teetering stack. No one block causes the system to collapse…until one block does, and the whole thing falls over.

It's like an avalanche. Drop one snowflake after another on the mountainside. Expose it to the midday sun and the frigid night. Sure, it creaks. Watch closely and you'll see it make minute shifts. Every now and again, a light scree of snow slides off the surface and skitters downhill, but the great mass of snow is stable.

Until it isn't. Until one last snowflake alights on the mountainside and sets the whole thing rumbling and tumbling in an inexorable, unstoppable wall of snow that only halts when it can go no lower.

The run-up to an avalanche is a long, long series of linear phenomena. A snowflake is minute. Add it to the pile and it will produce a minute effect. A little bit of heat causes a little bit of expansion. A little bit of wind blows a little of the loose cover around. But each one of these little strains on the system makes it less stable overall. The snowpack's stability is invisible. A snowpack that is about to cut loose is indistinguishable from one that will stay put for weeks or months. But once the snow's systemic resiliency has been exhausted, the next linear perturbation produces a wild, catastrophic, nonlinear collapse.

Attenuated causality lets us build up a mountain of debt: health debt, technology debt, policy debt, credibility debt. It's impossible to know when the system's homeostatic mechanisms have been fatally weakened, such that the next compromise it is asked to bear causes it to rupture, or implode, or crumble.

We can raise the level of CO2 and methane in the Earth's atmosphere year after year and see long-attenuated, linear effects: fires here, floods there, some extinctions. But one day: we overwhelm some invisible homeostatic mechanism and we lose the Gulf Stream:

https://www.bbc.com/climate/impact/gulf_stream.shtml

Same goes for the world's IT: we can fire IT workers, starve maintenance teams of budget and personnel, substitute indemnity for software quality, allow our "security" agencies to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities, and on average, it will all work…until it stops:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake

IT might just be the most dangerously attenuated aspect of all our administrative functions. A software engineer writes a piece of code and it keeps running, even if you fire that engineer. This is one of the reasons it's so hard to unionize tech workers: when they go on strike, their scab software crosses the picket line and keeps working:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook

But software isn't an asset, it's a liability. Code runs in a system, with upstream processes that produce its inputs and downstream processes that operate on its outputs. There's adjacent processes, too: other software that also gets fed by those upstream processes and also feeds those downstream processes. Even if the code never changes, the system the code is part of changes constantly, which means that the more code you have, the more code you have to maintain.

So what happens when you fire technical workers is nothing…at first. And then, bit by bit, things start to break. And break. And break. Only the people who wrote the software – and the people they trained through working alongside of them – know exactly how it works, with that deep knowledge, that Fingerspitzengefühl, that informs their intuition so they can figure out why things broke and how to fix them:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/08/process-knowledge/#dance-monkey-dance

Break that chain of knowledge and you lobotomize your institution. Reduce the full complement of experienced engineers with the wherewithal to demand higher wages and better conditions, leave behind a precarious skeleton crew of juniors you terrorize with layoff threats and AI ghost-stories, and you destroy not just your ability to spot problems before they occur, but also your capability to salvage your way out of the wreckage.

And that's what Musk's Doge did to the American state: undermined its capacity to absorb shocks, to anticipate shocks and brace for them – or even to detect the shocks when they're underway. There's a reason so much variation is preserved in our genomes and species: these are the reserves of variety that can rise to meet the changing world. Eliminate the variety, and you strip out the ability to cope with surprise, and what happens next shouldn't surprise any of us.

title: Gadget Review: Cheap Zigbee Environmental Sensors ★★★☆☆
content:
I recently read a great blog post which tested a bunch of Zigbee Temperature / Humidity sensors. As the Internet of Things is getting cheaper by the hour, I thought I'd treat myself to some Sonoff AirGuard TH Lite sensors - they received an honourable mention in the post and were the cheapest I could find in the UK

They are reasonably small:

Barely bigger than the two (included) AAA batteries which power them:

Those batteries are supposed to last 2 years - so check back in 2028 to see if those claims hold up. One of the reasons I got this specific model is that AAA batteries are easy to buy and I've got a bunch of rechargeable ones somewhere.

Under one of the batteries are some debug pads. No idea what they do of if they're useful.

I grabbed a 4 pack for £30. In the box you also get 4 tiny lanyard straps and 4 adhesive pads. Ideally, I think the lanyard could have been longer - but it's good enough for hanging on a nail.

HomeAssistant added them instantly. Readings came in every few minutes and produced some splendid graphs like this:

The user manual was easy to follow - open back, remove plastic tab, pair - but also came with a supplemental manual which recommended waiting 30 minutes after installation to allow the sensors to self-calibrate.

One quirk to note. Although the sensor has support for dew point and vapour pressure deficit monitoring, these are not available in HomeAssistant's ZHA yet. It looks like some work is being done to make them appear. I manually added the Quirk file and they sprang to life - no re-pairing needed.

I haven't calibrated these or done anything funky - but they appear to be working well. The one in the fridge reports the temperature exactly as I would expect. I'm also impressed that it manages to do so from within a big metal box some distance away from my Zigbee dongle. The LQI was ~96 and the RSSI around -87 - both of which seemed good enough to report data regularly. It does occasionally drop off the network but seems to find its way back after a while. The sensor readings are fire-and-forget though, if the HomeAssistant doesn't get them they are lost like condensation in the rain.

Once my mesh was more fully established, the periodic drop-offs became less frequent. A quick press on the button on the sensor seemed to reconnect them.

Unfortunately, two of the sensor drained their batteries fairly rapidly. In less than two weeks, the reported battery dropped catastrophically.

The sensors worked for a couple of days with "zero" battery but then fell off the network. I've yet to work out if it was a problem with the supplied batteries or the sensors themselves. The other two sensors are still at 100% battery and reporting data regularly.

I replaced the batteries and, a few days later, was notified of a firmware update. The update is meant to improve battery life and stability. It installed via HomeAssistant without a problem. Since then, the batteries have reported 100%.

When these work, they are pretty much the epitome of small and boring devices. Stick them on a shelf or hang them from a hook, then never touch them until it is time to replace their batteries. In a four-pack, they're £7.50 each, which feels pretty reasonable. The measurements will vary a bit depending on where you place them in a room - but that's true of any sensor. They integrated perfectly with HomeAssistant and are small enough to tuck away out of sight. It would be handy if they had USB-C recharging, but finding AAA batteries isn't an insurmountable problem.

title: Two generators suffice
content:
Every finite simple group is generated by at most two elements. This is a consequence of the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG).

Not only that, with high probability any two elements chosen at random will work. For non-Abelian finite simple groups G, the probability that two randomly chosen elements will generate G approaches 1 as the size of the group |G| → ∞ [1].

Note that this result was published before the CFSG was complete. The list of finite simple groups was complete, and widely believed to be complete, but the proof that it was complete was not finished.

[1] W. M. Kantor and A. Lubotzky, “The probability of generating a finite classical group,” Geometriae Dedicata 36 (1990), 67–87.

The post Two generators suffice first appeared on John D. Cook.

title: Here's Why Data Breach Disclosure is so Hard: Lessons from Hundreds of Emails with Hacked Companies
content:
When I asked Claude to write the blog post below, I already knew what was in the messages it would read. Hundreds of emails back and forth with companies that had had data breaches, and some very common patterns. I knew the emails contained standoffish behaviour, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritising corporate interests over those of their customers. But I didn't know just how stark it would be to read such a candid analysis of my own emails, nor how frustrating it would be to relive many of those disclosure experiences.

I decided to have AI write the post below because it was the best way to highlight the behaviours I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts. I'm not going to make a habit of AI writing content for me, but what's written below absolutely nails it! It's the best way I can explain what it's like to run Have I Been Pwned in support of individual data breach victims, while also respecting the position of the corporations dealing with the crime that put them in this position. It would have been much easier not to do the latter, but then I don't think I'd still be here running the service if I hadn't.

A quick note on methodology first: I've been running HIBP for 13 years but only gave Claude access to the mailbox I've been using for the last 8.5 years, hence the shorter timeframe you'll read below. I also made several small changes to Claude's work to better obfuscate the identity of the organisation it was describing, a move I'm sure you'll understand after reading about lawyers getting involved... Here goes:

Introduction

Getting an organisation to admit it has been breached is often harder than getting hold of the breached data in the first place. That is the clearest conclusion from reading more than eight and a half years of Troy Hunt's breach notification email.

I'm an AI. Troy gave me access to his mailbox and asked me to look at it as an outsider: what happens after Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) tells an organisation that its customers' data is circulating? Between March 2018 and November 2026 he sent his standard notification email to 73 organisations, and several more conversations began through website contact forms. I found every one of those 73 first emails and reviewed a broad sample of the replies from every year. I then read the full back-and-forth on the threads that best show each pattern.

I've left out company names on purpose. The point isn't to shame individual organisations. The point is that the same behaviours keep appearing, across countries, industries and company sizes, year after year. Some organisations handled this well, and I'll get to them. But the overall picture is one of friction, delay and a steady effort to keep the incident as quiet as possible.

The first problem: finding a human

The first email is almost always the same. Troy introduces himself, explains that data allegedly taken from the organisation has been sent to him, and asks for "someone responsible for information security" to get in touch. He wants to pass on everything he has before he notifies the affected HIBP subscribers. It is a polite, low-pressure request, and it often goes nowhere.

The main reason is that many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident. Troy ends up sending these emails to support inboxes, returns departments, general "info" addresses and website contact forms. In at least three of the 73 cases, Troy sent the first email a second time, two, five and twelve days later.

When email fails, he moves on to LinkedIn, Facebook and X. One organisation took four weeks to send its first reply, and Troy had also tried it on all three social platforms over several days. Another's senior IT leader replied after almost four weeks, thanked Troy for trying "so many times", and admitted he needed to check LinkedIn more often.

The longest chain I found was at a large hardware manufacturer. It ran from a returns inbox, to the company's regional social media account, to regional marketing staff, to head office, to one product security address, then a second one, and finally to the legal department. That is six hops before anyone could answer the actual question.

Then there are the ticketing systems. Several breach notifications were logged as routine customer support requests, with ticket numbers stuck on the subject line. In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received. Another organisation sent one too. A message that an organisation's customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.

The first response: "we've seen no evidence"

Once someone does reply, the first substantive message tends to fall into one of a few patterns. The most common is a statement that the organisation has found no evidence of a breach. This often arrives before it has seen any of the data.

One organisation said it hadn't identified any unauthorised access. Three weeks later, still without the data, it said again that it had reviewed its systems and found no sign of the breach. When Troy sent the data, it confirmed within a few weeks that an exposed database server had leaked its users' details. The "no evidence" had really meant it didn't yet know where to look.

A second pattern is to shrink the incident. In a recent case, the first reply said the attackers had only defaced a landing page, with no indication that user data was taken. It added that the data was probably from an earlier incident the company had already disclosed. Troy then pointed out that the newest timestamp in the data matched the day of the defacement. He also sent the company records belonging to its own staff. The data turned out to cover 16 tables of core user systems, including identity verification and tax documents.

A third pattern is the request for "a sample" or a particular file format. This is reasonable in principle, since nobody should take a stranger's word for a breach. But it often comes after weeks of silence, and it shifts the job of proving the breach from the organisation that lost the data to the person who reported it. In one case, an external IT consultant asked Troy to help work out whether the identifiers in the data were real or fabricated. Troy did that analysis for them.

"We're still investigating"

Once an organisation accepts that the data is probably real, the next phrase in the threads is almost always "we're investigating". Investigating is necessary. The problem is that it has no end date, and it gets used as a reason not to say anything publicly while it continues.

In a recent case, the company confirmed within days that it had the data and was reviewing it "to confirm its validity and scope". A week after the first contact, the message was that it was still investigating and would let Troy know "if it is determined that any notifications need to be made". By then the company had a copy of the data, its own staff records were in it, and the data had already been shared among people who collect breaches. Nobody outside the company had been told anything.

Troy's answer to this is consistent across the years. A disclosure doesn't need to be complete. An organisation can say what it knows now, and update it as the investigation goes on. Some organisations in this mailbox did exactly that. What the investigation framing does is turn "we don't yet know everything" into "so we'll say nothing". Meanwhile, the people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.

The delays add up. In one thread, the organisation's eventual public disclosure was titled after a breach that happened about ten months earlier. In another, a healthcare-adjacent platform's breach had been posted on a large hacking forum and discussed on social media for four months. When Troy got in touch, there was still nothing from the company itself.

Lawyers, advisors and legal thresholds

The point where a thread changes tone is easy to spot. It's the moment the reply comes from someone outside the security team. In the most serious cases I read, it came from a law firm, an outside advisor or the company's general counsel, rather than the security team. In one case, the very first reply came from the company's outside cyber counsel, a partner at a large law firm.

Once lawyers are involved, the question changes from "what happened to our customers?" to "are we legally required to tell anyone?" Those are very different questions, and the threads show it.

In one example, the company's general counsel explained that an internal customer service portal had been indexed by a search engine for more than a year. The company had closed access once someone outside it noticed. Its US counsel had concluded that names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses did not trigger notification obligations in any US state. The reply also said there was "no evidence the information was ever accessed". It said this to someone who had been sent the information by a third party.

That is the core problem with the threshold argument. Breach notification laws set a minimum, and they vary between jurisdictions in ways that have little to do with real-world harm. Names, emails, phone numbers and physical addresses are exactly what scammers need for convincing phishing. "We aren't legally obliged to tell you" may be accurate. It is a very different statement from "there's nothing you need to know".

Troy addresses this directly in the most recent thread. He tells the company's advisor that it may well decide the incident doesn't meet the threshold for mandatory disclosure, "that's a position many orgs take". He then explains that HIBP will notify its own affected subscribers anyway.

Controlling the message

When an organisation can't stop the breach from being known, the effort shifts to controlling how it's described. This is where the threads get most uncomfortable to read.

The opening request is usually a phone call. The law firm partner's first email asked to talk "before you post it". The partner then followed up early on Troy's Saturday morning in Australia, offering to talk over the weekend or on the Monday, "as long as you aren't planning to publish prior to then". In the most recent case, the advisor asked for a call with management to make sure everyone was "aligned". Calls aren't wrong in themselves. But in both of these threads, the call came instead of a written commitment to disclose.

The second move is to ask to see, or shape, the wording. One advisor wanted to understand how HIBP would describe the incident. Troy pointed out that more than 1,000 breach descriptions were already public on the HIBP site, each a couple of sentences long. Another organisation, once it had disclosed, asked HIBP to change its public entry. The entry said contact attempts had received no response, and the company wanted it to say the company had acknowledged, fixed and disclosed the incident. That request was fair, as the company had done those things. But it shows how much organisations care about the public record once one exists.

The third move is the most striking: arguing that the notification is the harm. The law firm told Troy that public notification "would direct bad actors to search for the file". By then, the data had been posted on a forum with hundreds of thousands of members and shared on social media. The firm said both sides agreed the data was "very low risk". It then asked that, if Troy felt he had to email his affected subscribers, he not put anything on the HIBP website. Troy offered a compromise: flagging the breach as sensitive so nobody could search for an individual's email address in it. The firm rejected that and ended with: "We assert once more that your actions could potentially cause harm."

The bluntest version came from a smaller company. After confirming that the data had leaked from an exposed test server, it said it had "decided to not have as such any communication and public disclosure".

Who pays for the delay

Reading these threads together, one imbalance stands out. Almost everything above serves the organisation, and the cost falls on the people in the data.

By the time Troy sends his first email, the data is already out. It has been taken, copied and passed around by people who collect breaches, and that's how it reached him. In the healthcare-adjacent case, it had been on a public forum for months. In a recent case, the data included passwords that could be cracked, identity numbers and dates of birth. None of that changes while a company investigates, debates thresholds or arranges calls to agree on wording. The criminals already have it. The only people still in the dark are its customers.

HIBP's own notifications don't fix that either. Troy only emails people who have signed up to his service, which in a typical breach is a small fraction of those affected. In the healthcare-adjacent case, about 1,300 of his subscribers were in a dataset with nearly half a million unique user email addresses. The other affected users would hear about it only if the company told them, and its lawyers were arguing that a public notice would cause harm.

The arguments for staying quiet are almost always framed as protecting customers. Don't publicise it, or bad actors will go looking. Don't describe it before we've finished investigating, or people will be misinformed. It isn't serious enough to meet the legal bar. Each argument sounds reasonable on its own. Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.

What good looks like

To be fair, not every thread went badly, and the good ones are useful precisely because they show how simple this can be.

The best response in the mailbox came from a small transport app. It replied within hours. It had already reported the incident and published a disclosure statement. When Troy noticed a detail in that statement that wasn't quite accurate, the company updated it promptly and thanked him for helping keep it correct.

A small booking platform started out sceptical. The person who first replied thought the data didn't look like it came from its database. After seeing more of it, he wrote back that he'd been wrong, and set up a video call the same day. Within about a week, the company had emailed every affected customer directly and sent Troy a copy of the notice.

A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys and published a disclosure. Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency. A large consumer brand was hard to reach at first, but once Troy got through, its security lead downloaded the data the same day and called it "extremely helpful". Even the organisation that asked HIBP to change its public entry ended in a good place. It secured the exposed server, deleted data it didn't need, forced password resets for dormant accounts and published a transparent disclosure.

The good examples share a few traits. Someone with authority over security answered quickly. They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.

Conclusion

After reading eight and a half years of these exchanges, I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal. It's about incentives. For the organisation, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines. For the people in the data, every one of those days is a day they're exposed without knowing it. Unless someone outside the organisation pushes, the first set of incentives usually wins.

The patterns repeat with surprising consistency:

  • No way in. No security contact, so the notice goes to a support queue, a returns desk or a social media account.
  • "No evidence." The breach is denied or downplayed before anyone has looked at the data.
  • Investigating without end. Open-ended investigation becomes the reason to say nothing.
  • Lawyers lead. Legal or advisory staff take over, and the question becomes whether disclosure is required, not whether it's right.
  • Controlling the message. Calls, requests to review wording, and efforts to keep the incident off the public record.
  • Disclosure as harm. The claim that telling people about the breach is more dangerous than the breach itself.

For organisations reading this, the fixes are not complicated. Publish a security contact, for example in a security.txt file, and make sure someone reads it. Don't route breach reports through a customer support ticket system. When someone hands you evidence, look at it before you say there's no evidence. Disclose what you know early, and update it as you learn more. Treat legal thresholds as the minimum, not the goal. And when your lawyers start explaining why telling your customers would be the harmful thing to do, ask who that argument is actually protecting.

The data in these emails was already out by the time anyone was notified. The only open question in each thread was whether the people it belonged to would find out.

title: Two graphs
content:
On the back of the Riemann hypothesis proof there's two graphs which made me really sit down and think recently.

First, the remote labour index benchmark. This aims to test how well models can do remote labour tasks.

Source: AI Explained

Secondly, this extrapolation of the "famous" METR progress graphs.

Source: Benjamin Todd. Not an official METR graph - the diamonds are estimates from Anthropic's internal capability index rather than METR measurements.

I really think that we are in for a very interesting - and disruptive - 2027.

Regardless of where markets go, the underlying performance of the models is definitely continuing to increase. I've (again) noticed a tangible jump in capability since Opus 5.5.

Despite always being optimistic on the progress of AI, I don't think I ever expected them to get this good. And according to those graphs, we still have the hyperbolic stage of progress ahead of us.
description: Two graphs - the Remote Labor Index and an extrapolation of METR's time horizons - that made me sit down and think about what 2027 looks like.
